newsitem.title: BOSNIA: US envoy meets Bosnian leaders.
newsitem.headline: US envoy meets Bosnian leaders.

text.p: U.S. envoy John Kornblum held talks with Bosnian political leaders over the weekend to discuss the country's peace process and international efforts to promote democratic reforms in neighbouring Serbia.
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum met the Moslem chairman of the collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, on Saturday evening after arriving in Sarajevo.
Kornblum told Izetbegovic about results of a major powers' Contact Group meeting in Brussels which focused on a wave of opposition protests in Serbia, state television reported.
The Group ruled out imposing international sanctions on Serbia but agreed individual countries would consider ways of exerting pressure on authoritarian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Western governments say events in Serbia, which backed the Dayton peace accords on Bosnia, could have a significant effect on postwar events in the former Yugoslav republic.
Kornblum attended a conference on post-war economic policy in Sarajevo on Sunday morning and was due to meet leaders of Bosnia's Serb republic later in the mountain village of Pale, outside Sarajevo.
Kornblum planned to raise the issue of the disputed northern town of Brcko during his weekend tour, a U.S. embassy official said.
The first arbitration session to settle its future status opened in Rome earlier this week with U.S. lawyer Roberts Owen presiding.
The strategic town is considered a volatile flashpoint that could reignite fighting between Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic.
Both sides have staked out divergent positions. The Bosnian Serbs, who captured the Brcko corridor early in the war, say the area must remain under Serb control.
The federation says any solution to the dispute must be based on the town's pre-war population, in which Moslems and Croats formed a majority.
Separatist Serb forces backed by neighbouring Serbia expelled Moslems and Croats from Brcko when they seized the town early in the 1992-95 war.
